claim: On 14 June 2024 the US Department of Health and Human Services, through the Administration for Community Living, released 'Aging in the United States: A Strategic Framework for a National Plan on Aging', developed by leaders and experts from 16 federal agencies working through the Interagency Coordinating Committee on Healthy Aging and Age-Friendly Communities, laying the groundwork for a national plan on aging.
source_note: Found via search for the HHS/ACL Strategic Framework. The primary acl.gov pages returned HTTP 403 to automated retrieval, so the National Institute on Aging's repost of the HHS news release (which reprints it in full) is the working source.

claim: S.2120, the Older Americans Act Reauthorization Act of 2025 (119th Congress), was introduced on 18 June 2025 by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) with Sen. Bernard Sanders (I-VT) among the cosponsors; it passed the Senate without amendment by unanimous consent on 14 July 2026 and was received in the House on 15 July 2026.
source_note: Found via search for the Older Americans Act reauthorization. The canonical congress.gov bill page returned HTTP 403 to automated retrieval, so the official GPO/Library of Congress bulk-data bill-status XML (the same underlying record, which links back to congress.gov) is the working source. It is machine-readable XML rather than a human-readable page.

claim: On 19 December 2024 ARPA-H launched the PROactive Solutions for Prolonging Resilience (PROSPR) program, led by program manager Andrew Brack, to develop therapies that extend healthspan in older adults, including identifying physiological and biochemical markers of early health changes during aging.
source_note: Official ARPA-H news release, found via search for ARPA-H aging programs. The program funding total appears on the later award announcement (see us-004), not this launch page.

claim: On 24 February 2026 ARPA-H announced the seven research teams funded through its PROSPR program — including Stanford University, UT Health San Antonio, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, Cambrian BioPharma and University of Rochester — with the program investing up to $144 million over five years in healthspan-extension research.
source_note: Official ARPA-H award announcement, found via search for the PROSPR program. Per-team award amounts are not disclosed on the page.

claim: The National Institute on Aging's FY 2025 congressional justification requests $4,425.3 million for NIA, an increase of $13.2 million over the FY 2023 final appropriation of $4,407.6 million, with aging research named among the administration's priorities.
source_note: NIA's FY 2025 congressional justification page, found via search for the NIA budget; the companion PDF is dated March 2024, so a year-only source date is used. The page shows the President's Budget request, not the final enacted FY 2025 appropriation.

claim: On 12 February 2025 the US Senate Special Committee on Aging, chaired by Sen. Rick Scott (R-FL) with Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) as Ranking Member, held the hearing 'Optimizing Longevity: From Research to Action' (S. Hrg. 119-40), taking testimony from witnesses including Buck Institute for Research on Aging CEO Eric Verdin and Blue Zones founder Dan Buettner.
source_note: Official GPO-published hearing record, used because the committee's own aging.senate.gov page returned HTTP 403 to automated retrieval. Medium confidence on classification: a committee hearing is a congressional document but not a bill, so 'political statement' is also arguable.

claim: On 25 April 2025 six members of the US House of Representatives — Gus Bilirakis, Paul Tonko, Dan Crenshaw, Ro Khanna, Scott Peters and Sam Liccardo — announced the re-launch of the bipartisan Congressional Caucus for Longevity Science, which aims to educate Members of Congress about the growing field of aging and longevity biotechnology.
source_note: Official House press release on Rep. Bilirakis's site, found via search for a congressional longevity caucus. The release's own member list mislabels Rep. Khanna's state, so the claim omits party/state labels.

claim: Jim O'Neill, a longtime longevity advocate who was CEO of the SENS Research Foundation from 2019 to 2021, was sworn in as US Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services on 9 June 2025. He has written of aging: 'More and more influential people consider aging an absurdity. Now we need to make it one.'
source_note: Secondary source (MIT Technology Review), used because no directly retrievable primary HHS or Senate page supporting the longevity framing was found (congress.gov nomination pages blocked automated retrieval). The quoted line is from the 2020 SENS Research Foundation annual report as cited by the article.

claim: In March 2025 the National Institute on Aging announced the launch of the Exceptional Longevity Translational Resources (ELITE) Portal, an NIH-designated data repository centralizing data from NIA-funded studies of exceptionally long-lived people — including the Long Life Family Study, Longevity Consortium, Longevity Genomics and Integrative Longevity Omics — to accelerate research on the biology of exceptional longevity.
source_note: Official NIA blog post by Chhanda Dutta, Chief of NIA's Clinical Gerontology Branch, found via search for NIH exceptional-longevity resources. Classified as policy (an agency infrastructure decision); the underlying studies are NIA-funded, so funding is also arguable.

claim: On 29 July 2026 the trans-NIH Geroscience Interest Group (GSIG) and the National Institute on Aging announced the Fifth Geroscience Summit, 'Revisiting the Geroscience Hypothesis – Focus on Health', for 2-3 December 2026, convening scientists, clinicians and policy experts around geroscience — the field studying how the biological mechanisms of aging contribute to chronic disease, aiming to extend healthspan.
source_note: Official NIA blog post by Viviana Perez Montes, Director of NIA's Division of Aging Biology. Medium confidence on classification: an agency-convened scientific summit is recorded as policy (agency program activity) for lack of a better-fitting label in the schema.

claim: In accordance with the RAISE Family Caregivers Act of 2017, the Administration for Community Living published the 2022 National Strategy to Support Family Caregivers and opened a 60-day public comment period (Federal Register notice of 6 October 2022, comments due 30 November 2022) to inform the ongoing work of the Family Caregiving Advisory Council.
source_note: Official Federal Register notice (87 FR 60684), found via search for the RAISE Act national caregiver strategy. The strategy document itself lives at acl.gov/CaregiverStrategy, which blocked automated retrieval.

claim: On 6 January 2021 Governor Gavin Newsom's administration released California's first-ever Master Plan for Aging, a ten-year blueprint with five bold goals for 2030 — including 'Health Reimagined' and a target of one million high-quality caregiving jobs — as the state's 60-and-over population grows toward 10.8 million by 2030.
source_note: Official California Health & Human Services Agency announcement, found via search for the California Master Plan for Aging. The plan originated from Governor Newsom's Executive Order N-14-19 (June 2019); the plan portal is mpa.aging.ca.gov.

claim: On 4 November 2022 New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed Executive Order No. 23 creating the state's first-ever Master Plan for Aging, directing the Health Commissioner and the Office for the Aging Director to head a Master Plan for Aging Council developing guidance for healthy, livable communities for older New Yorkers.
source_note: Official New York Governor's office press release, found via search for the New York Master Plan for Aging executive order.

claim: On 30 June 2025 Governor Hochul released New York's first-ever Master Plan for Aging Final Report, containing more than 100 proposals across nine pillars including healthcare modernization and caregiver support; the FY 2026 state budget includes $45 million in additional funding for community-based aging services through Area Agencies on Aging.
source_note: Official New York Governor's office press release, found via search for the New York Master Plan for Aging. The full report and proposal library are at planforaging.ny.gov.

claim: Montana's 69th Legislature (2025) enacted SB 535, an act revising laws related to experimental treatments, providing for licensing of experimental treatment centers and amending the state's Right to Try Act; it covers treatments that have successfully completed phase 1 of a clinical trial but are not yet FDA-approved.
source_note: Enrolled bill (authorized print version, session-law chapter file CH0621) on the Montana Legislature archive; text extracted and checked locally. Year-only date because the signing date (12 May 2025 per secondary coverage) is not in the bill text. The law is widely discussed as a legal basis for longevity clinics, but that framing comes from secondary coverage, not this source.

claim: Colorado's HB22-1035, 'Modernization of the Older Coloradans' Act', signed into law on 24 March 2022, expanded the state Commission on Aging from 17 to 19 members and created the Lifelong Colorado initiative within the state office on aging to coordinate implementation of Colorado's strategic action plan on aging.
source_note: Official Colorado General Assembly bill page, found via search for Colorado's strategic action plan on aging. Status: signed by governor, effective 24 March 2022, session laws chapter 38.

claim: Minnesota released its Multisector Blueprint for Aging in December 2024, a ten-year state plan produced through the Age-Friendly Minnesota Council created by Governor Walz's Executive Order 19-38 in December 2019; one of its four domains is 'Optimized Health and Longevity'.
source_note: Found via search for the Minnesota Multisector Blueprint for Aging. The primary mn.gov/dhs pages and PDF are behind bot protection and could not be retrieved, so the Age-Friendly Minnesota Council's own site is the working source — the official initiative site but not a .gov domain, hence medium confidence.
